performers: Kerstin Thorborg, contralto; Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam; Carl Schuricht (live; Carl Martin Öhmann sings the tenor songs of the same concert)
intro: “Von der Schönheit” (Comodo. Dolcissimo) is the fourth movement of Das Lied von der Erde. Girls pick lotus flowers by a river; horsemen ride past, and one girl watches after them. Kerstin Thorborg sang it in this 1939 performance in Amsterdam.

sections.mNote: Flutes and muted violins open in G major.

sections.label: C · March for brass, drums and mandolin
sections.mNote: Brass, drums and mandolin play a march

cues.title: Opening in G major
cues.text: Trilling flutes and muted violins open the movement in G major. Thorborg’s first words are “Junge Mädchen pflücken Blumen” (young girls pick flowers). The melody moves between bars of two and three beats.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Das Lied von der Erde, Universal Edition full score (1912), pp. 61–62: Comodo. Dolcissimo, the opening scoring and changing metre. Hans Bethge’s text as adapted by Mahler; our translation. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/65/IMSLP20582-PMLP47886-Mahler_-_Das_Lied_von_der_Erde_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Sources of the poem
cues.text: The poem descends from Li Bai’s “Lotus-plucking Song”, set at Ruoye Brook near Shaoxing. The Marquis d’Hervey de Saint-Denys put it into French, Bethge into German verse, and Mahler retouched Bethge’s text. Li Bai’s original is far shorter than the song.
cues.evidence: Mahler Archives, Von der Schönheit page, prints Li Bai’s poem and the location of Ruoye Brook, d’Hervey de Saint-Denys’s “Sur les bords du Jo-yeh”, Bethge’s text and Mahler’s alterations: http://www.mahlerarchives.net/Archive%20documents/DLvDE/Der_Schonheit.htm

cues.title: Zephyr stanza, solo violin
cues.text: The harmony moves from G major down to E major. The violins remove their mutes, and a solo violin plays above the words about the breeze lifting the girls’ sleeves. The harp plays chords beneath the long vocal line.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition full score (1912), pp. 63–64: rehearsal 5, a tempo (ruhiger), Dämpfer ab and the solo violin beside the Zephyr stanza.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Orchestral interlude before the horsemen
cues.text: Thorborg finishes on “Luft” — air — and the orchestra takes over, Allmählich belebend. Stopped horns and muted trumpet and trombones enter over harp glissandi. The voice is silent until the horsemen stanza (rehearsal figures 7–10).
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 65–70, rehearsal figures 7–10. Allmählich belebend follows the end of the breeze stanza; the voice remains silent until the horsemen stanza.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: March section with mandolin
cues.text: The march adds a mandolin to the drums and brass. The tambourine rattles, bass drum and cymbal mark the beat, and both harps play chords.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 67–68: Più mosso subito (Marschmäßig), mandolin, two harps and percussion.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Horsemen stanza, voice
cues.text: The orchestra drops to p subito for the singer’s return: “O sieh, was tummeln sich für schöne Knaben” (see the handsome boys romping there). Timpani played with wooden sticks keep the rhythm of the hooves, and the vocal part becomes faster and more crowded.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 70–77: Noch etwas flotter, p subito, Holzschlägel and the increasingly rapid horsemen stanza. Bethge’s text as adapted by Mahler; our translation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mahler’s changes to Bethge’s text
cues.text: In the lines about the horse Mahler added words that are not in Bethge: “Hei! Wie flattern im Taumel seine Mähnen, dampfen heiß die Nüstern!” (how his mane flies in a frenzy, how hot the nostrils steam). He also changed the word for the girl’s pride from “Lüge” (lie) to “Verstellung” (pretence).
cues.evidence: Mahler Archives, Von der Schönheit page, prints Bethge’s text beside Mahler’s alteration: the mane and nostril lines are absent from Bethge, and Lüge becomes Verstellung: http://www.mahlerarchives.net/Archive%20documents/DLvDE/Der_Schonheit.htm . Translation by the site.

cues.title: Return of Tempo I, rehearsal 16
cues.text: The text describes the horse’s flying mane and steaming nostrils. At rehearsal 16 the opening tempo returns subito (Tempo I, Andante). Muted violins and harp play, and Thorborg repeats the words “Gold’ne Sonne” — golden sun.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, p. 77, rehearsal 16: Tempo I subito (Andante), muted violins and the return of “Gold’ne Sonne webt um die Gestalten”. Our translation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final stanza, “Ganz ruhig”
cues.text: In the text, the girl’s proud bearing is a pretence; her eyes follow the rider, and her heart still trembles after he has gone. Mahler marks the passage “Ganz ruhig” (quite calm). Clarinet phrases and the violins continue beneath Thorborg’s last words.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 78–80, rehearsal figures 19–22. The final stanza and its quiet clarinet and violin writing; translation of Mahler’s tempo marking.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Carl Schuricht, Wiesbaden and Amsterdam
cues.text: Carl Schuricht, born in Danzig in 1880, was Wiesbaden’s music director from 1912. He conducted the Eighth Symphony there in 1913 and gave Mahler weeks in 1920 and 1921. He conducted this performance in Amsterdam on 5 October 1939, by which time Mahler’s music had vanished from German concert programmes.
cues.evidence: The Wiesbaden Stadtlexikon entry on Schuricht gives his birth in Danzig on 3 July 1880, his appointment as municipal music director in 1912 and his Mahler programmes (the Symphony of a Thousand in 1913, Gustav Mahler weeks in 1920 and 1921): https://www.wiesbaden.de/en/microsite/stadtlexikon/import/a-z/schuricht-carl . The Internet Archive item gives the Amsterdam concert of 5 October 1939: https://archive.org/details/06-das-lied-von-der-erde-mahler-concertgebouw-amsterdam-carl-schuricht-5.-x.-193 . Erik Ryding’s Library of Congress essay on the 1938 Ninth notes that Mahler’s music was disappearing from concert programmes after a pattern set in Germany: https://www.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/MahlerSymphonyNo9.pdf

transitions.title: Unmuted violins and E major
transitions.from: A · Comodo, G major, flutes and violins
transitions.to: B · Silk sleeves in the breeze, E major
transitions.how: A ritardando closes the image of sunlight reflected in water. At rehearsal 5 the music resumes in E major, a minor third below G, marked a tempo (ruhiger). The violins take off their mutes. Their high melody and the woodwinds’ little turns lead into the breeze stanza.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition full score (1912), pp. 63–64, rehearsal 5: E-major signature, a tempo (ruhiger), Dämpfer ab and solo violin.

transitions.title: From the voice’s “Luft” into the march
transitions.from: B · Silk sleeves in the breeze, E major
transitions.to: C · March for brass, drums and mandolin
transitions.how: After the voice’s final “Luft”, flute and violins hold high notes above the harp. At Allmählich belebend the orchestra begins to move. Stopped horns, muted trumpet and trombones enter, and the harp plays a glissando in D major. The march accelerates to a C-major harp glissando (Universal Edition score, pp. 65–68, figures 7–9).
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 65–68, rehearsal figures 7–9: D-major and C-major harp glissandi, brass entries and the march.

transitions.title: Voice returns over wooden-stick timpani
transitions.from: C · March for brass, drums and mandolin
transitions.how: At rehearsal 10 the march, heavy with brass, drops to piano subito and the voice returns. At Noch etwas flotter, Thorborg names the horsemen over oboes, clarinets, bassoons and strings. Timpani played with wooden sticks mark the rhythm beneath her line.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition score, p. 70, rehearsal 10: vocal return, p subito, Noch etwas flotter and timpani with Holzschlägel.

transitions.title: Return to Tempo I with muted violins
transitions.how: The racing vocal line ends on the words about the horse’s steaming nostrils. At rehearsal 16 (Universal Edition score, p. 77), Tempo I subito (Andante) brings back the muted violins, followed by the harp and a solo violin. The return begins under a signature of two flats. The G-major signature comes back in the following system, with the words about golden sunlight on the water.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition score, p. 77, rehearsal 16. The return begins with two flats before the G-major signature returns in the following system.

transitions.title: Ganz ruhig and the orchestral ending
transitions.to: Coda · Clarinet and violins after the voice
transitions.how: The words about the girl’s pretended pride give way to Ganz ruhig. Quiet violin figures descend while the clarinets exchange short phrases. The final vocal line ends in G major. The winds and strings continue its small gestures into the closing bars.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 79–80, rehearsal figures 19–22: Ganz ruhig, clarinet phrases, violin figures and the orchestral ending.

source.title: Mahler, Das Lied von der Erde, IV. Von der Schönheit, full score (Universal Edition, 1912, plate U.E. 3637)
source.locator: Printed pp. 61–80: the river scene, horsemen’s march and quiet return. The march also includes a mandolin.

timeline.note: Trilling flutes, a horn and muted violins open the song.
The alto enters over soft woodwinds, harp and muted strings.
Ruhiger: piccolo, horn and glockenspiel as the girls gather blossoms.
The violins remove their mutes as E major arrives; harp chords support the woodwinds.
A solo violin plays above the strings at the breeze and the perfumes.
After “Luft”, stopped horns and muted trumpet and trombones enter above a harp glissando.
A C-major harp glissando and brass with open bells begin the horsemen’s music.
The march: timpani with wooden sticks, bass drum, tambourine and brass.
Thorborg returns at piano, with woodwinds, strings and timpani played with wooden sticks.
Allegro without voice, with flutter-tongued flutes, trombones and tuba, and strings.
Trumpets play above the percussion and the strings’ galloping figures.
The alto returns for the neighing horse, with springing bows in the violins.
Tempo I subito: muted violins, solo violin and harp return with the words about the sun on the water.
At Ganz ruhig, quiet violin figures and clarinet phrases accompany Thorborg’s last lines.
The voice has finished; woodwinds and harp play fragments of the opening theme.
Harp harmonics and low strings play a final ppp chord.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Kerstin Thorborg (contralto), Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam (orchestra), Carl Schuricht (conductor)
fields.note: The item credits Kerstin Thorborg (alto), Carl Martin Öhmann (tenor) and Carl Schuricht (conductor) for the whole concert, and names the singer on each track; Carl Martin Öhmann does not sing in this song. The Mahler Foundation’s discography lists the same three with the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam. The orchestra was not yet styled “Royal” in 1939.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Music by Gustav Mahler (died 1911); words adapted by Mahler from Hans Bethge’s Die chinesische Flöte (Bethge died 1946), itself a paraphrase of Tang-dynasty poems by way of French and German translations. The 1912 first edition is hosted on IMSLP as public domain.
fields.note: A term calculation (life plus 70 years; Bethge’s text has been free in life-plus-70 jurisdictions since 2017), not a clearance of every edition or translation.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Treated as public domain in the European Union (territorial): a live broadcast of 5 October 1939 whose related rights, on the sources consulted, had expired before the extended terms applied on 1 November 2013. United States status is not established.
fields.note: Before the 2011 extension, Directive 2006/116/EC gave performers and phonogram producers 50-year terms. For a performance of 1939 the performer’s term ran 50 years from the performance, to 1989, unless a fixation of it in a phonogram was lawfully published or lawfully communicated to the public within that period, which would have started a longer term from that event. The live radio broadcast was a communication of the performance, not of a phonogram fixation, and the sources consulted document no earlier publication of the acetate fixation; the date of its first issue on disc is not given in them, so this is an inference, not a clearance. Directive 2011/77/EU lengthened terms to 70 years only for rights still protected on 1 November 2013 (Article 10(5)), so rights that had already expired were not revived. The item carries a Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s statement and not the basis used here.

composer.epithet: Conductor who composed during the summers and intended each symphony to contain a whole world, combining the sublime with the music of the street band.

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. In Iglau he heard bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church, and these sounds recur throughout his music. Late in life he told Sigmund Freud that he had once run from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was playing Ach, du lieber Augustin.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition, and he sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. Among his friends were Hugo Wolf and Hans Rott, who died young. Rott’s symphony is so close to Mahler’s own music that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. By then he had already begun his career as a conductor, and that career would pay for everything else.
